<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 61>
                                              Abstract

Management of Medical Records and Clinic Tasks
Medical documentation, medical appointments, and day-to-day management of your clinic are often
done via different channels. Patients may not be able to monitor their medical documentation in a clear
way. The clinic staff will not able to work on the same documentation of the patients. MyHealth Care
is a prototype of a health-care-management system, developed using Flutter and Dart, during a senior
project at the University of Bahrain. The MyHealth Care app has separate interfaces for the patients,
the doctors, and the admin, allowing them to view medical histories, upload records, book
appointments, record consultation notes, manage prescribed medications, and manage admin and
doctor staff tasks. It also has the right-to-left interface with dual language (English/Arabic) support.
The app employs Riverpod for state management and effectively isolates screens and business logic
from the repository interfaces. Local data persistence relies on Drift and SQLite, with the version-35
database (reviewed, here) containing 69 related tables with migrations, foreign keys, and some, but not
all, integrity controls. A separate Node.js API underpins the limited shared-server pilot, but it does not,
yet, support all workflows. The project also includes rule-based clinical flags, demonstration AI
summaries, and a logistic-regression predictive model of appointment no-shows, but these are all
currently disabled for live clinical use, as they have not yet been clinically validated.
Integrity and foreign-key errors were not found on an inspection of the supplied synthetic SQLite
database. The repository has many automated tests, but I was unable to execute the whole Flutter test
suited to completion during my technical review. Overall, this project demonstrates how all aspects of
patient data and clinic operation can be brought together in one app. Care should be taken to
understand that this is an academic prototype created using synthetic information and is not a system
that should be used for any actual patient care. Future work would include user testing, shared
deployment, and formal review before any clinical deployment.

                                          Chapter 1
                                         Introduction
Health systems are responsible for keeping the information correct but also allow for the day-to-day
operations that need to be performed, such as scheduling appointments, checking results, and saving
notes from a consult. These operations are likely to be far more complex if medical history,
appointment information and staff activity are stored separately. Patients may struggle to access
historical records, doctors may need to search across multiple locations prior to seeing a patient, and
administrators will need to follow-up with users on things like booking requests and operational
instructions. MyHealth Care was created to research how this kind of operation could be performed as
simply as possible in a single application, while accommodating different roles and permissions.
The original project proposal focused on three key questions: how can medical records be displayed in
a way that makes a helpful patient summary (RQ1); how can scheduling appointments and predicting
no-shows be done, and what steps might be improved (RQ2); and how can staff be helped to identify,
prioritize and structure tasks that matter (RQ3). These questions therefore provided the overall design
direction. The end system, while comprising extra support functions, are not documented herein and
what the code and the available testing evidence support should not be assumed to already mean that a
functioning university prototype has resulted in improved clinical results.

1.1 Problem Statement
Sub-problem 1 — Incomplete medical history. A patient probably has consultation notes, lab
results, prescriptions, vitals, as well as reports that are uploaded at disparate points of time. The
objects displayed on separate screens or locations makes the history difficult to follow. By specifying
Medical Records to Lab Values, Document Files and review information and showing in the timeline
Medical Records, Data imported/ stored in or imported from the prototype along with their origins and
review status is displayed. The prototype demonstrates Medical Records integration and does not
interface or connect to the hospital records outside of the prototype.
Sub-problem 2 — Appointment Scheduling. The system needs to determine if the selected doctor is
available given their schedule and exceptions, it is not enough to simply display an empty time slot
since another user can request the same slot before user confirmation. MyHealth Care determines
available time slots based on the schedule and exceptions and also assesses the appointment request
based on these. It sends an idempotency key to prevent double booking if the same request is
performed twice. Confirmed appointments may be message queued but the reduction in actual no-
shows and the delivery to a sleepy app has not been proven.
Sub-problem 3 — coordination amongst clinical staff. Doctors, nurses, receptionists and
administrators each perform specific tasks and should not necessarily have access to the same set of
medical data. Therefore the webapp includes a role-specific workspaces and verifies access to relevant



                                                                                                      1
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 9 / 61>
patient data and tasks. It also has rule-based validation of some selected observations to produce flags
and follow-up tasks. Staff can view who is responsible for tasks and task progression. These are role-
specific processes, but the rules have not been approved to allow for diagnosis or clinical triage. The
project is therefore confined to a role-based demonstration of record set, appointment set and tasks to
staff, with clear boundaries to data accessibility and data storage and automated process.

1.2 Project Objectives
The main goal is to create and test a health-care-management prototype that allows the patients to get
their information and help clinic staff in handling appointments and day-to-day management. The
objectives are summarized in functions that can be verified by the code and corresponding test cases:
  1.    Patient-centered data modeling: the users, patients, staff, departments, appointments,
        records, laboratory values, prescriptions, consultation, and billing data were organized
        systematically in a well-structured manner into different associated tables in the database. The
        relationships can be verified through schema, migration, and foreign-key check.
  2.    Role-separated experience: The GoRouter acts as a community resource for each user
        (patient, staff, administrator) and screens for an active session and additional permissions to
        use protected routes or view certain records.
  3.    Records management: The app shows the clinical records in chronological order and allows
        patients to upload supported files. It uses SHA-256 fingerprints to detect duplicate files and
        keep track of whether a clinician has already viewed an imported record.
  4.    Appointment management: User can find any doctor, check the availability of slots, fix an
        appointment, and track the status. The system should check for the limits on schedule,
        duplicate bookings, and multiple attempts.
  5.    Consultation and pharmacy workflows: Clinicians can save draft consultations and
        complete signed notes and medication orders using controlled database operations but will
        also have a record of all subsequent changes made.
  6.    Staff coordination: The system automatically detects the various risk conditions based on the
        existing rules and generates the relevant tasks that are capable of task assignment, escalation
        and completion with history.
  7.    AI research: AI Research The platform shows offline summaries and performs no-show
        prediction experiment. We ask you to report inputs and synthetic evaluation results, but not
        including them as evidence of clinical validity.
  8.    Usability: The application provides interfaces in both English and Arabic and supports right-
        to-left flow and flexible layout on multiple screens. The key user flows are observed on
        Mobile and Desktop.




                                                                                                        2
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 10 / 61>
  9.    Quality assurance: Maintains integrity of unit, widget, database, integration and back-end
        tests within the development process. It is important to note which tests were directly run and
        which were the result of reports from previous repositories.
Project scope. The sanctioned demonstration runs in Chromium using synthetic data stored on the
device. Although native app files and a shared Node.js server pilot have been included, multi-device
operation is incomplete, and the Demonstration will not prove hospital record exchange, or real bank
card processing, or certify a clinical decision. These areas will need development and certification.

1.3 Relevance/Significance of the Project
Patient experience. One patient workspace helps you find appointments, captured observations, and
documents. To share with family, access is controlled with specific links and permissions. A link will
specify if access is to be by way of a representative on the software, but this does not specify the
legally appointed guardian.
Clinical operations. Booking checks, consultation states and staff task history improve the
traceability and testability of each operation step and are likely to diminish the inconsistencies in
application states. Whether they less average waiting times, or help decrease clinical errors, would be
another study, with real users, and a sanctioned methodology.
Software engineering. The app specifies each of the Flutter screens, Riverpod providers, repository
interfaces, and database implementations. This architecture allows for testing core rules even without
depending exclusively on the interface, as well as for future changes in storage or services. It also
complies with the guidelines of dividing responsibilities of the application in Flutter guide and ISO
software quality model (Flutter, n.d.; ISO/IEC, 2023). The choice of disabling unvalidated AI features
is an intentional preference for safety.
Broader relevance. Digital health solutions could increase access to information and facilitate
connectivity if issues related to privacy, interoperability, and institutional support are also incorporated
into development of technology (World Health Organization, 2021b, 2025). MyHealth Care explores
how this could be achieved with an English/Arabic university prototype. To make a meaningful
contribution, the project will demonstrate a viable design, content, and implementation, not increase in
health outcomes.

1.4 Report Outline
Chapter 2 describes the survey of related research in electronic records, patient portal, scheduling,
decision support, interoperability and privacy issues. Chapter 3 explains the development process,
defines risks involved in the project and proposes the items to be done. Chapter 4 stipulates
requirements, personas and models of the system. Chapter 5 states the architecture, database schema
and interface design. Chapter 6 introduces implementation process and the results of testing. Chapter 7




                                                                                                          3
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 11 / 61>
makes a conclusion, addresses the limitations and factors for future work. List of references is
presented after the last chapter.

<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 12 / 61>
                                        Chapter 2
                                    Literature Review
2.1 Introduction to Digital Healthcare Management Systems
Digital systems for healthcare management are used for storing clinical data and for tasks like booking
appointments, assessing results and communicating with patients. For a system to be usable it needs to
do more than simply store files digitally; it should present information in an understandable way, be
available to those who need to access it and be part of normal everyday activities. Earlier studies have
explored these issues in several contexts such as electronic health records, patient portals, reminders
and clinical decision support systems. The MyHealth Care prototype combines certain functionalities
from these fields within a common, university-based example.
This chapter looks at each relevant field according to the project criteria and looks at and summarizes
each peer-reviewed academic article and technical standard that is relevant to each theme of the
project. For each theme the techniques used, the results obtained and the shortcomings of the
techniques, results and conclusions presented by the previous researchers are summarized. Emphasis
will be placed upon evidence relevant to the three aims of the project: care record presentation;
appointments management and staff facilitation.
Studies made in a hospital environment or on dedicated clinical platforms cannot be directly
extrapolated to this project. MyHealth Care uses synthetic data and has not been tested on regular
patient care environments. The existing literature helps clarify design decisions and provides suitable
testing methods, rather than claiming a similar outcome for this application.

2.2 Digital Transformation and Electronic Health Records
Electronic health records (EHRs) are a collection of diagnoses, prescriptions and tests, all of which are
stored electronically. In an analysis and systematic review of 62 individual studies Campanella et al.
(2016) found some measures of health care quality increased following EHR implementation. But the
effect of EHR adoption differed from one individual measure to another and is important: storing data
electronically doesn't automatically indicate that the data implementation was effective at improving
clinical decision-making.
Kruse et al (2018) examined the use of EHRs for population health, finding benefits and real-world
challenges of EHR adoption and data utilization for population health. On another review, Kruse et al
(2016) discovered reasons for poor EHR adoption, including cost, technical issues and staff resistance.
Both papers seem to suggest that a database and interface is only part of an EHR project, as
organizations need working workflows, data accuracy and organizational change support.
MyHealth Care addresses one aspect of the bigger picture. Its Medical Records, Lab Values, and
uploaded files are related to patient records and are viewable in a timeline view. The benefit shown
here is the ability to access these records in an easy-to-view way in the application. There is no
confirmed importation from a hospital EHR, and the project has not measured any change in quality of
clinical care. Literature provides strong evidence for the reasonableness of developing a single,
cohesive view of the record, and at the same time shows that interoperability and acceptance are still
problems.




                                                                                                       5
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 13 / 61>
2.3 Patient Portals, Mobile Health and Patient Engagement
One way that patient portals help ease the burden is that they offer a different way for people to access
health information and some services without necessarily having to reach out to a clinic for each
individual item or task. According to Irizarry et al. (2015), "simply providing access isn't enough:
users have very different levels of digital skills, health literacy, and motivation to engage online, and
what may work well for an advanced user might challenge a user who is uncomfortable with
physician-designed vocabulary and computer questions."
Goldzweig et al. (2013) investigated the evidence for electronic patient portals. While many studies
had reported benefits with individual features, the evidence regarding overall improvements in health
outcomes was disappointing and inconsistent. This is important to MyHealth Care as while a timeline,
booking page and notification view will bring all services together, the report must not state that
patients would have a better knowledge of their conditions until the evidence is obtained by testing the
use of the product.
Mobile apps also have their own set of complexities regarding usability, content, and privacy
considerations. Marcolino et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review of systematic reviews of mobile
health solutions and found that there were benefits with their use in some circumstances, but the
review process and outcomes were heterogeneous. Nouri et al. (2018) showed that a user-centred
approach to the evaluation of a mobile health application requires more than simply focusing on its
surface characteristics. These findings suggest that in addition to responsive layout, accessible record
details, and providing bilingual (Arabic and English) display messages, MyHealth Care should address
an evidence gap by conducting a usability study with representative patients (including older patients
and those with disabilities who rely on assistive technology) with this prototype.



2.4 Appointment Scheduling, No-Show Behavior and Reminder Systems
Absence from a scheduled appointment results in the inefficient use of available clinic slots and in
some circumstances delays in follow-up treatment. Dantas et al. (2018) reviewed 105 outpatient no-
show studies and found an average non-attendance rate of around 23% in the reviewed studies.
Anamnesis of past missed appointments and longer waiting times between booking and appointment
time were the most cited factors. While this data offers some relevant background, it is not a recorded
rate for Bahrain or for the MyHealth Care members.
Reminders consider the problem from a different angle. Hasvold and Wootton (2011) reviewed
research pertaining to SMS and telephone reminders, and the majority of studies have shown that
reminders improved attendance, but that the effects and cost benefits will be dependent on a particular
environment. A prediction score can flag an appointment as likely to be missed, and a simple reminder
or an easily rescheduled option is a response the patient can make. The current research has not
supported that an in-app reminder will notify the patient after the application has been closed, the
delivery system itself will need separate validation.
Moreover, MyHealth Care has a technical scheduling problem that is different from predicting no-
shows. The booking repository needs to validate the schedule so overlapping bookings don't occur,
even when a user makes duplicate bookings of the same user input. Appointment Repository
Impl.book() validates the schedule and accounts for exceptions and existing schedule intervals in a
transaction with an idempotent result. A predictive model has been trained to predict no-shows using




                                                                                                       6
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 14 / 61>
logistic regression, but it is not yet enabled for operational use. Subsequent tests should focus on
validating the booking, reminder delivery, and prediction accuracy as a simple performance indicator.



2.5 Artificial Intelligence, Predictive Analytics and Health Summarization
Clinical data is a valuable source for prediction and information extraction. Shickel et al. (2018)
survey of deep-learning research in medical data using electronic health record data, various potential
clinical uses of this include prediction and patient representation. They note that challenges also arise
from noisy, sparse data, as well as low interpretability, a wide variety of datasets. This research scan
offers valuable contextual information from a technical perspective, but one should bear in mind that a
model that is successful in one study sample will not necessarily be successful in other medical
environments or patient populations.
In addition, researchers are studying the use of large language models in answering medical questions
and creating summaries. Singhal et al. (2023) measured medical knowledge and responses with three
multiple choice datasets and a panel of physicians. While the results were encouraging under certain
test conditions, neither they nor the team demonstrated overall clinical safety. Ghassemi et al. (2021)
wrote that a "fluent language system may make a medical AI explanation seem more credible even if it
is inaccurate, indicating that these systems can generate fluent but not medically correct summaries".
In addition, choice of training data and prediction targets is very important. Obermeyer et al. (2019)
showed that a healthcare algorithm produced inaccurate results when using healthcare expenditure as a
surrogate for illness. Wiens et al. (2019) listed four components of responsible medical machine
learning, including appropriate evaluation, continuous monitoring, and careful design of workflows.
MyHealth Care's no show prediction model was based on synthetic appointments. It is unknown
whether this can validate fairness or accuracies in real patient populations, or whether it can is
effective in decreasing missed appointments. It is wise to leave the tool and other live clinical AI off
until these questions are definitively solved.



2.6 Clinical Decision Support and Staff Workflow Coordination
Clinical decision support systems uses or models are used by clinical decision support systems to
deliver contextually appropriate information to clinicians. Sutton et al. (2020) reviewed the emerging
benefits and dangers of failed implementation, which focused on too many alerts and an
overdependence on machine-based suggestions. A warning is only useful if it is sent to the right
person who can respond to it. This highlights the need for simple to understand rules and for staff to be
empowered to make and record the ultimate decision.
Sittig and Singh (2010) delineated a sociotechnical model, which impels the consideration of
healthcare software with users, tasks, and organization within which this software operates. Their
model comprises concepts, but not rigorous evaluation of a particular application. It explains the
concept of a correct laboratory threshold: helpful alerts require correct input, lack of ownership,
escalation procedures, and documentation of the subsequent steps.
MyHealth Care uses the Risk Detection Service to run predefined checks on the selected observations,
whereas Task Repository Impl performs the corresponding tasks. Every task has an owner, state and
history; access is role and care relationship based to ensure it is as constrained as possible for audit-
trail concerns (Sutton et al. 2020). The threshold values have not yet been clinically validated nor have



                                                                                                       7
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 15 / 61>
these alerts been cross-examined for fatigue. Subsequent testing should include a review of each rule
by a qualified individual, and consideration of both missed alerts and false alarms.

2.7 Health Information Interoperability and Data Standardization
Even if it is well-structured, however, an internal database may be solved in a way that prevents it
from interacting with other healthcare systems. Lehne et al. (2019) examined the concept of
interoperability in digital medicine and acknowledged that differences in data formats and semantics
can severely restrict data interoperability. While placing a patient's data in such structured SQLite
tables makes them easy to use in MyHealth Care, they would not be automatically understandable by
the hospital's EHR system.
Mandel et al. (2016), allows healthcare applications to connect to electronic records by providing
standard web-based interfaces. This is an example of a technically feasible solution that could help
overcome some of the barriers described by Lehne et al. (2019). It should be kept in mind that
standards do not solve all these issues, and organizations will have to agree on how they identify users,
what users can access what records, and how they interpret information from other sources.
MyHealth Care is using local Drift/SQLite and has a trial API in a different Node.js implementation. It
does not have a verified SMART on FHIR connection to a clinical provider. At some point in the
future, we may start out with a set of FHIR Patient, Appointment, Encounter, and Observation
resources with source identifiers and review status, before exchanging real patient data we will also
need good patient matching, authorization, consent, and clinical data validation procedures in place.

2.8 Healthcare Information Security, Privacy and Ethical Governance
Protecting medical records There is much more in protecting medical records than just password
screens. Keshta and Odeh (2021) summarized the security and privacy issues in electronic health
record (EHR) systems, including violations to confidentiality and data control. In the MyHealth Care
system, every time access to a page should be validated, data are also validated when queried or saved.
Therefore, distinguishing local demonstration data from a server where real patient's data would be
stored is the crux of its security.
In addition, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) raises another responsibility. Wiens et al. (2019) have
argued that medical machine-learning algorithms should have "well-specified goals, adequate
evaluation, and continued monitoring." The bias found by Obermeyer et al. (2019), which has been
confirmed by our third example, demonstrates how one total metric of accuracy can hide differences
between groups of individual patients. These have not occurred even in the simple case of using the
model only to rank tasks.
The public MyHealth Care program should continue to focus on using synthetic data. Its shared-server
pilot program is unfinished, and it has yet to gain approval to host real patient information. Although
the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act is an example of US health care standards, it
does not specify the rules in Bahrain. A real implementation would require an audit of local
legislation, organizational policies, security procedures and clinical duties.

2.9 Usability, Accessibility and Bilingual Healthcare Interfaces
Healthcare screens can be susceptible to usability issues due to unfamiliar terminology, date,
measurements and what may be to one action could have different weightings of importance. Zahabi et
al. (2015) completed a review of research on the usability of electronic medical record interfaces, and
identified common themes related to consistency, display of information, errors and mental workload.


                                                                                                          8
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 16 / 61>
They concluded that an ideal screen would help users find important information rapidly and clearly
describe the outcomes of any actions.
Nouri et al. (2018) identify many aspects of mobile health quality, whereas Irizarry et al. (2015) focus
on inequities in users' ability to make use of digital services. Together, these works support interaction
with effective tasks rather than assessing the interface's design. For example, users need to be able to
find laboratory results, find out whether the imported record has been approved, and correct recording
errors when booking.
MyHealth Care are available in English and Arabic with right to left formatting. These are a good first
step for Bahrain, but simply having a version does not mean Arabic medical terms will be understood
or mixed Arabic / English numbers, dates and screen-reader focus are working properly. It would be
worth testing the main patient and staff journeys in both languages, including large text and keyboard
only.



2.10 Challenges in Existing Solutions and Research Gaps
Results of studies in this review, mostly good, generally show that ease of access to health information
is supported but the literature suggests the successful installation of software does not necessarily lead
to a successful implementation. Campanella et al. (2016) found improvements in some EHR-related
measures and Kruse et al. (2016) found it can be a barrier to adoption; Goldzweig et al. (2013) have
weak evidence of specific outcomes for Patient Portals. All these findings make sense as it may be
helpful technology in some cases but can also be problematic.
Second, the studies highlight the separation between prediction and intervention. For instance, Dantas
et al. (2018) lists predictors for missed visits while Hasvold and Wootton (2011) list reminder
intervention but neither suggests that using a risk score can act as an intervention to stop a missed
visit. Similarly, Shickel et al. (2018) and Singhal et al. (2023) propose the promise of AI and then
Ghassemi et al. (2021), Obermeyer et al. (2019), and Wiens et al. (2019) describe the need for a
careful evaluation of the AI's effectiveness and detection of bias before putting it to the use.
A further concern, or at least potential problem, exists in systems interoperability and who is
responsible for decisions. Fragmented health data (Lehne et al., 2019), standards-based integration
(Mandel et al., 2016), and the human and organizational context of safety (Sittig & Singh, 2010) are
discussed. MyHealth Care doesn't have the solutions for all these ongoing problems, but it does serve
to demonstrate a unified structure for patient records, appointment validation, access policies, and staff
accountability within one role-based prototype.
The sources use varied research methods, which will color their conclusions. Meta-analyses boil down
what is found in other sources, however, are limited by their underpinning studies. Technical and
standards-based literature will suggest a way of working that could be adopted without evidence of a
change in outcomes for patients. Work on bias will explore possible ways of failure, but the measured
effects may be different in some contexts. For this reason, this review will use literature to support
design choices and highlight questions that remain, rather than attempting to claim generalizability to
MyHealth Care.




                                                                                                        9
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 17 / 61>
2.11 Summary of Literature Review
Other evidence shows both the value and the issues of digital medicine. Electronic records have the
potential to help structuring clinical data, but worries remain over uptake, usability, and connectivity
(Campanella et al., 2016; Kruse et al., 2016; Lehne et al., 2019). Patient portals and mobile apps can
simplify access to healthcare, but the research on their outcomes is not consistent (Goldzweig et al.,
2013; Marcolino et al., 2018). Digital medicine studies on missed visits recommend on-going
assessment of scheduling and reminder systems to improve attendance (Dantas et al., 2018; Hasvold
and Wootton, 2011), and studies on clinical artificial intelligence call for thoughtful processes for
realizing technology's full potential (Obermeyer et al., 2019; Wiens et al., 2019).
The results align with MyHealth Care's three main goals: bringing together information, providing
rock-solid schedule booking, and helping staff manage later tasks. MyHealth Care illustrates all three
with its bilingual Flutter app and its local relational database. The experiments with predictions and
the AI showcases act as research tools, not yet as officially sanctioned clinical services. Additional
development is needed in practical user evaluation, secure shared deployment, legacy/connected
interoperability, and medical review.




                                                                                                     10
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 18 / 61>
                                      Chapter 3
                                 Project Management
The application was constructed in phases, with features being implemented and tested as the
application matured. The proposal, source code and project checklists are evidence of this. Despite the
lack of formal Scrum meeting minutes and completed sprint reports, these documents enable the
nature of the work to be described as an iterative development. This chapter explains the development
methodology, key risks and activities.

3.1 Process Model
3.1.1 Iterative and Incremental Development Approach
The incremental method takes a big task and divides it into little, doable portions. The primary
dependencies for MyHealth Care were for consumer roles, navigation, and information associations.
We used those to construct patient information and reservation making features, then added the
clinical and administrative workflows. With every addition, we needed to confirm the validation,
authorization, and database behaviors that accompanied that capability. It felt like we did the right
factor because the different displays relied on the same customers, appointments, and scientific
information.
The repository outlines 6 broad phases of work; first, the flutter app set-up with routing, sharing of
error handling, dependency injection and first database; second, construction of patients' accounts,
profiles, notes, and booking; third, construction of staff screens with schedules, consultations, results
review, and Tasks; fourth, construction of documents, pharmacy, billing, audits, and retry controls;
fifth, construction of rules-based risk checks, AI experiments, and improvements to Arabic, English,
and responsive layouts; lastly, construction of tests, security, and limited shared-server API. These are
the observable phases of development; they are not claimed to be conventional dated Scrum sprints.

3.1.2 User-Centered Design and Continuous Validation
Established signs of continued refinement include the DESIGN.md, database migrations up to v.35,
the automatically generated Drift and Freeze files, test suites, and two project review checklists. Taken
together these documents suggest features were tackled and bugs were fixed iteratively. The proposal
also forecasts over a 16-week timeline. Because the records do not all include both sprint dates and
team velocity data, I am employing the proposed timeline as a project planning guideline rather than
as a measure of when each task was completed.

3.1.3 Quality Gates and Definition of Done
This was noted as ready to review when its requirements were documented, the databases and
repository code had been created, and the main screen was able to perform that action. For sensitive
actions, that involved the permission checks, rejected input, and repeated requests all in the same
operation. For booking and consultation functions, extra care needed to be taken to note that a failed



                                                                                                      11
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 19 / 61>
write did not leave inconsistent records. Checklist items are useful pointers to progress, but the
existence of a checklist item does not replace a reproducible test result.

3.1.4 Scope Control and Change Management
With the development of the application, additional projects included the three research questions as
well as features related to billing, issued documents, pharmacy, and workforce. The amount of
integration work increased significantly. For the university demonstration, we felt it was necessary to
separate out functioning that is mandatory and whether shared-server features and clinical features are
optional, so we are able to take new requests only when we have time to implement and test the new
features without impacting on the main work of the patient and staff.

all based on a qualitative engineering judgment rather than any quantitative chance of an event
occurring. The table includes typical development risks as well as privacy, authorization, and clinical-
decision risks, all of which are critically relevant in a healthcare app.

3.2.1 Risk Monitoring and Control
Risk monitoring was achieved through specific tests and repository review checklists. Significant tests
included 1. Patient permissions check, 2. Duplicate booking check, 3. Database migration check. The
checklists also identify unapproved items such as clinical and privacy checks and the extensive shared-
server deployment, which are identified as open items even after the related software feature has been
released.
In Flutter, most of the interface code is shared, but the security and storage aspect can behave
differently on web and native devices. In this project, local storage is used with Drift/SQLite and there
is a second pilot running with a Node.js API. Firebase is not used as the main database.

The stages are divided up into five planned sets of the work: requirements and literature review in
weeks 1-3; design in weeks 4-6; implementation in weeks 7-9; testing in weeks 10-12; report write up
in weeks 13-16. These are mapped to the available set of materials in table 3.2. These week numbers
are only taken from the original plan and are not exhaustive.

3.3.1 Requirements Collection and Literature Planning
The plan of the project included all information about patients, clinicians, administrators, the main
research questions, initial privacy concerns, and literature review, which can be found in its entirety as
Chapter 2.

3.3.2 Architectural and Database Design
The design section for weeks 4-6 covered the design of the use cases, user roles, database
relationships, navigation and initial interface. The design document and schema show the output of
these design steps, but do not specify the specific times when each was completed.

3.3.3 Implementation and Feature Integration
It was scheduled for weeks 7-9. First, the main patient and clinical screens were created, using Flutter,
Riverpod, and the local repository layer. Other modules such as documents, pharmacy, billing, and
workforce, were added in later releases, and required more integration work.

3.3.4 Testing and Quality Assurance
Testing was planned for weeks 10-12, but documentation in the repository shows testing continued as
the project grew larger. Unit, widget, database, and API tests were written to test different parts of the
application. This report distinguishes between tests that were directly monitored during the technical
review, and test results documented earlier by the project team.




                                                                                                                                        15
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 23 / 61>
3.3.5 Deployment and Demonstration
The supported deployment has just a browser demonstration with synthetic data. There is a separate
pilot for the shared API which is not complete for all features. Therefore, the graduation
demonstration should demonstrate repeatable workflows for patients, doctors, and administrators
rather than declare the system ready to handle real clinic records.

3.3.6 Documentation, Presentation and Release Review
Final project activities are made up of system reports, diagrams, screenshot and presentation. The
same tasks also require ensuring the written statement true to the working features. Accessibility in
Arabic and formal review on privacy, security and shared deployment are still the activities which
have yet to be assigned up to date before probable use outside the university.
For a reproducible release check, the team should record their versions of Flutter, Dart, and Node, run
analyzers and tests, build the web app, and check database upgrades with data. Manual checks should
include both language versions, major user journeys, accessibility, and handles for failed or
unauthorized actions. Better evidence is provided than by a checklist of features when these checks
have been done.



3.4 Chapter Summary
The repository demonstrates continuous development via functional features, reviews and tests. An
iterative development approach enabled local patient/staff workflows to be refined as demands arose.
During the final university demo, the key goal is to produce a stable and approved scope and show
evidence of the tests performed.

<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 24 / 61>
                               Chapter 4
                   Requirement Collection and Analysis
4.1 Requirement Elicitation
4.1.1 Stakeholder Identification
The proposal mentions three main user types: patients, hospital staff and administration. It also
presents three needs: make records easier to access, make appointments easier to manage, make
clinical follow-up easier to organize. Those needs were compared with screens, domain models, and
repository contracts of the application. The project documentation and testing have also been used for
additional information on permission, errors, and the expected change of state.

4.1.2 Data Collection Methods and Evidence Boundaries
Available elicitation evidence. There is little elicitation evidence. The artefacts provided with this
project do not include any survey results, interview transcripts, enumeration or consent records.
Therefore, there are no interviews or questionnaires presented as activities within this report. The
stated needs have been derived from the proposal, the paperwork, and the realized artefacts. Any
separately gathered user research must be reported with its actual methodology and conclusions.

4.1.3 Domain Analysis and Requirement Prioritization
Traces were taken from the proposal, DESIGN.md, two review checklists, repository interfaces, and
scenario tests. Every major function was written out with the person doing it, the pre-conditions that
should be true before it, and the post-conditions after it. For example, booking requires permission to
administer the patient, an available clinician that passes all criteria, an available time slot, and checks
against double booking. Access to a medical history requires the correct identity of the patient, results
in chronological order, and clear information of the origin of a record.
The original proposal described general ideas like AI assisted summaries, intelligent scheduling. The
actual implementation distills out some of these ideas to ones that can be shown safe: imported and
synthetic records, rules-based staff task management, and an experimental no-show model that isn't
used in scheduling decisions. In the requirements tables we mean 'implemented locally' to refer to the
Drift/SQLite version of the function, and 'partial shared' to mean that the server-backed
implementation is only partial.

4.2 System Requirements
4.2.1 Functional Requirements
Table 4.1 lists functions found in the application and identifies the relevant user roles. The
requirement IDs were assigned for this report to help relate requirements to the implementation; they
are not claimed to be original project issue numbers.

HIPAA is a United States healthcare privacy and security framework and does not automatically
certify a student application in Bahrain (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, n.d.). Its
principles can still inform access control, logging and protection of medical information. Before using
real patient data, the project would need a separate review of Bahrain's applicable legal and clinical
requirements. The prototype is not presented as compliant or certified for clinical deployment.

4.3 Personas
The following personas describe typical tasks for each user group based on the application design.
They are illustrative examples, not profiles of people who were interviewed during the project.

4.3.1 Patient Persona
Persona P1 — Patient, 34, uses Arabic and English on a phone. The patient wants to check
previous laboratory results, view appointments and share selected information with a permitted family
member. A typical journey is Home → Medical Records → Record Details, or Book Appointment →
Choose Doctor → Confirm. Important concerns are unclear medical terms, unexpected changes to an
appointment and not knowing whether an uploaded document has been reviewed.




                                                                                                                         20
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 28 / 61>
4.3.2 Clinician Persona
Persona P2 — Doctor, 42, mainly uses a desktop or tablet. The doctor reviews the day's
appointments, opens an authorized patient chart, records a consultation and finalizes the note. The
main requirements are fast access to relevant history, clear identification of unreviewed information
and protection against accidental duplicate orders or edits to signed notes.

4.3.3 Nursing and Care Coordinator Persona
Persona P3 — Nurse or care coordinator, 29, works with intake forms and a task queue. Daily
work includes recording observations, following up overdue tasks and handing work to another staff
member. The screen needs to show priority, current owner, task status and history so that urgent work
is not lost or repeated.

4.3.4 Administrator Persona
Persona P4 — Administrator, 38, manages users, departments, service requests and billing
exceptions. The administrator needs clear operational information and an audit history for sensitive
changes. The role should not automatically provide access to every patient's detailed clinical records.

4.4 System Models (Object-Oriented Approach)
The object-oriented models show how the main user actions relate to domain entities, repositories and
application services. Generated Drift or Freezed classes are treated separately from repository
interfaces written by the team. A database foreign key shows an association between records; it does
not necessarily mean the corresponding Dart objects have an inheritance or composition relationship.

4.4.1 UML Use Case Diagram Description
The use-case diagram defines the main MyHealth Care application boundary. Patient, staff and
administrator actions are carried out through Flutter screens. In local demonstration mode, the data are
stored in the client's Drift database. The optional shared mode connects to a Node.js service, which is
responsible for enforcing permissions on server requests. Notification, document and AI services
support selected use cases rather than acting as independent healthcare users.
The main actors are Patient, Doctor/Clinician, Nurse, Pharmacist, Reception Staff and Administrator.
A patient may use selected functions for an accepted linked family member when the required
permission exists. Supporting services include notification delivery, the simulated payment gateway,
optional Gemini integration and the shared server. AccessPolicy and the patient's clinical relationship
determine which records a staff member is allowed to open.

                    Patient/clinician                                           Live AI unavailable by capability

Figure 4.1 shows the main actions available to each user group. It is a summary of permitted
workflows, not a statement that every logged-in user can access every record. Family-linked actions
require an accepted relationship and the appropriate scope.

                           Figure 4.1: MyHealth Care UML use-case overview by actor

4.4.2 Process Specifications
Use case: Booking an Appointment
UC07 — Book Appointment. Goal: create a single authorized booking for a free clinician slot.
Preconditions:   active   session;   patient    account    or    valid   delegated    manage   relationship;
clinician/schedule exists; chosen start/end are valid. Main flow: (1) patient selects specialty/clinician,
visit type and day; (2) rankedSlotsProvider invokes AppointmentRepository.openSlots and shows
available chronological slots because operational no-show ranking is disabled; (3) user confirms; (4)
booking_providers.dart rechecks subject/proxy rights and submits BookingRequest with idempotency
key; (5) AppointmentRepositoryImpl.book() checks version, schedule/exception and interval overlap
inside a transaction; (6) appointment row and ticket metadata are committed, associated
reminders/outbox records are prepared, idempotency result is recorded; (7) UI receives
Ok(Appointment) and navigates to confirmation. Alternative A1: booked/conflicting interval → Err
with no appointment. A2: authorization revoked → access failure and no write. A3: same key retried
→ previous committed result, not a new row. A4: reminder dispatch temporarily fails → booked visit
remains committed and delivery is retried according to outbox semantics. Postcondition: exactly one



                                                                                                         23
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 31 / 61>
durable local reservation for the successful idempotency scope; no claim of cross-device serializability
in disconnected local mode.

Use case: Viewing Medical History
UC03 — View Medical History. Preconditions: valid session and patient subject access. Main flow:
(1) patient opens timeline/records; (2) the application resolves own or accepted linked subject; (3)
records_providers.dart calls an authorized record repository; (4) RecordRepositoryImpl filters by
patient identity, retrieves ordered MedicalRecords and associated LabValues/DocumentFiles
metadata; (5) screen groups records by date/type and indicates provenance and review status; (6)
details open the selected record and preserve patient scope. Alternatives: empty records show an
empty state; a revoked family link or foreign record ID is rejected; a missing file displays an error
rather than implying an attachment. Postcondition: no mutation is required for ordinary viewing,
except an authorized read-tracking action when invoked. Browser local data is not equivalent to
external hospital truth.

Use case: Patient Registration
UC02 — Patient Registration. Preconditions: user is signed out and registration enabled. Main flow:
enter required identity/contact details and password; screen validates input; AuthRepository creates an
account and patient profile with role-appropriate defaults; application returns explicit success or
transitions to sign-in. Alternatives: duplicate account identifier, malformed fields, weak/invalid
password and persistence failure must not result in a partially activated account. Postcondition: a local
account and associated profile exist when registration succeeds. The local demonstration does not
verify official national identity, government registry status or ownership of a real clinical record.

Use case: Importing and Reviewing Medical Records
UC04/UC05 — Import and Clinician Review. Preconditions: patient or managed proxy has access;
supported source file supplied. Main flow: collect record type, date, issuer and PDF;
RecordRepositoryImpl.add(NewRecord) validates file and issuer requirement, computes SHA-256,
applies per-patient duplicate logic, writes record, lab child rows and DocumentFiles atomically, marks
uploaded content pendingReview and produces audit/review work; authorized clinician later reviews
and accepts or rejects through reviewImport. Alternatives: unsupported/oversized file, duplicate
fingerprint without override, disallowed account, inconsistent lab data or failed transaction.
Postcondition: original byte provenance and review decision remain traceable; unreviewed user
uploads must not be presented as verified clinical truth.

Use case: Consultation and Signed-Note Finalization
UC09/UC10       —     Consultation     Finalization.    Preconditions:     authorized    clinician,     valid
encounter/appointment relationship and correct visit state. Main flow: open staff schedule and
consultation; load patient context; save EncounterDraft notes and draft medicines with version; invoke
EncounterRepositoryImpl.finalize; validate authorship and appointment state; run a transaction



                                                                                                          24
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 32 / 61>
creating deterministic SignedNotes and related medical/medication rows, mark encounter completed,
resolve walk-in linkage when applicable, remove the draft and write audit/outbox and idempotency
outcome. Alternatives: stale version, staff without relationship, invalid medicine fields or duplicate
finalize request. Postcondition: signed record is preserved against ordinary edits; later corrections are
additive SignedNoteAmendments rather than silent overwrites.

Use case: Managing Staff Tasks and Risk Flags
UC11 — Staff Risk and Task Handling. Preconditions: assigned staff and valid patient scope. Main
flow: RiskDetectionService collects recent vitals, records and medications; deterministic rules identify
threshold anomalies, missed follow-up or medication gap and derive deduplication keys; task
generation associates a source episode and owner; board groups urgent, overdue, today, upcoming and
completed    work;    an   authorized     user   acknowledges,   transfers,   escalates   or   completes;
TaskRepositoryImpl checks ownership/version and records TaskHistory. Alternatives: identical source
episode is deduplicated; unauthorized coverage cannot change task; stale version yields conflict; risk
rules yield no actionable finding. Postcondition: work has an accountable status and history. The
output is decision-support demonstration only.

Use case: Medical Document Issuance
UC12 — Document Issue and Verification. Preconditions: permitted template and issuer/role
conditions; related patient/appointment records exist where required. Main flow: prepare request,
submit, approve; DocumentServiceImpl.issue() snapshots patient, issuer, language, disclosure and
template content into IssuedDocumentVersions; separate rendering writes DocumentArtifacts with file
hash; delivery event is recorded; a recipient downloads an authorized version and verifier can check
minimal status. Alternatives: request rejected, credential not approved, render failed, version revoked
or superseded. Postcondition: immutable issued snapshot and reliable failure status; real-world legal
validity is not established solely by these software controls.
The key sequence for booking is BookingScreen → Riverpod provider → AppointmentRepository →
AccessPolicy → database transaction → appointment and idempotency records → result shown in the
UI. Consultation finalization follows a similar pattern, using EncounterRepositoryImpl to validate the
draft and write signed records, prescriptions and related updates together. Notification records are
prepared after a successful state change; their presence does not guarantee external delivery.

4.4.3 UML Class Diagram Specification
The domain layer defines Dart models and repository contracts, with concrete classes implementing
those contracts. Appointments refer to patient and staff accounts through identifiers; records are
related to laboratory values and uploaded files; staff tasks refer to owners and history entries.
PatientProfiles and StaffProfiles extend Users in the relational database through one-to-one links, not
through Dart class inheritance. AppointmentRepositoryImpl and RecordRepositoryImpl implement
their respective repository interfaces.



                                                                                                      25
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 33 / 61>
Table 4.4: Core class/interface responsibilities and relationships
                     Principal
 Class / interface   attributes or     Main methods / operations              Relationships
                     state
Repository interfaces define operations that the rest of the application can call, while concrete
repositories provide the database or HTTP behavior. Freezed generates model features such as equality
and copyWith; Flutter and Riverpod provide widget base classes. These generated or framework
classes should not be counted as additional business modules created specifically for MyHealth Care.




                        Figure 4.2: Representative UML class and repository interaction model

Figure 4.2 presents the main classes and contracts involved in appointment booking. It illustrates how
the booking logic depends on a repository interface and on explicit permission and replay checks. The
diagram is intentionally limited to the classes needed to explain this workflow.
Several rules govern changes to stored data. Appointment statuses follow controlled transitions, while
signed notes and issued-document versions are protected against ordinary overwrites. Version fields
help detect conflicting changes. A valid foreign key alone is not sufficient for authorization: for
example, a referenced staff account must also have permission to perform the requested clinical action.

4.5 Chapter Summary
This chapter connects the three proposal questions with the actions implemented for patients,
clinicians and administrators. The use cases describe normal activity as well as invalid inputs, denied
access and conflicting updates. The object-oriented models show how the application separates data
and business operations. Formal user acceptance and clinical validation would still be needed before
the system could be used outside the synthetic demonstration.




                                                                                                    26
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 34 / 61>
                                            Chapter 5
                                          System Design
This chapter describes the design in the source code currently in place. MyHealth Care, in fact, can be
tested with a local demonstration using synthetic data and there is a different implementation of shared
server with only some of the functionality. These two modes have different responsibilities in terms of
storage and access control and must be represented separately in architecture and deployment
diagrams.

5.1 Software Architectural Style

My Health Care has a layered, feature-first Flutter architecture. Screens and reusable widgets are
found   in   lib/features/presentation,      Riverpod   providers   and   workflow   definitions   are   in
lib/features/application. Domain models and repository contracts are in lib/domain; Drift and remote
implementations in lib/data; shared services like scheduling, access checking, risk detection, document
processing are in lib/services. The architecture is close in spirit to MVVM, as state management is
done outside the widget tree. However, I would say 'layered architecture with repositories and
Riverpod' is a better team than MVC.
It also allows testing and modification. For example, you can replace the repository interface with a
mock implementation for unit testing, which allows testing a specific rule without starting a complete
screen. You can also largely isolate modifications to the database or API by changing its adapter.
Importantly, checks for access are performed by the data and service layers, rather than by hiding a
menu item. These benefits only hold if you are disciplined about always following the repository
contract in each storage mode.
Some areas of the project are incomplete and require attention. Repository sizes are sometimes too
high, some screens depend on the specifics of the local database, and some shared-server adapters are
still not available. The dependency flow that is ideal is presentation to application to domain to
interface to data implementation. Flutter recommends responsibility separation and for data access to
reside through interfaces (Flutter, n.d.).
Access control lives on many levels. Session Controller guards the user log-in, router. Dart secures
routes, and Auth Context exposes the current account state. Before sensitive actions are taken, Access
Policy is checking roles, patient IDs, care-team relationships, family permissions, and other grants.
Some data streams check permission anew each time they update. All that makes the local prototype
more consistent, but browser-based security is not a replacement for a trusted server if real patients
and many devices are being used.
The local database is also built with Drift and SQLite and has migrated to the current schema version
35. The native app uses encrypted local storage, while the browser demo keeps its SQLite data in



                                                                                                         27
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 35 / 61>
browser storage without protection. The Node.js API has a separate server database of its own. The
outbox, idempotency, help us with retrieving and notifications, but not with full two-way sync
between browser and server.


Figure 5.1 — Layered architecture




Layered local and shared runtime architecture

                            specification
Medical-record flow. A patient opens the timeline or records screen. A Riverpod provider calls
RecordRepository, which checks the patient's access and uses Drift queries to retrieve
MedicalRecords, LabValues and related file or review information. The provider then updates the
interface. In shared mode, a supported remote adapter can call the Node.js API instead. If that function
is not implemented remotely, the application returns an unavailable result rather than pretending the
local data are shared.
Appointment flow. The patient selects a clinician and a displayed slot. Before saving,
booking_providers.dart confirms the patient or family permission and sends a BookingRequest.
AppointmentRepositoryImpl.book() checks schedules, exceptions and conflicts inside a database
transaction. It also checks the request's idempotency key, assigns ticket information and saves the
appointment. Reminder or outbox records are created for later processing, after which the UI shows
the booking result.



                                                                                                                             29
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 37 / 61>
Consultation flow. An authorized clinician opens an appointment, reviews the chart and saves a draft
note. Finalization checks the appointment and staff permissions, writes the signed note and related
medication or medical-record data, and updates the encounter in one transaction. Later corrections are
stored in SignedNoteAmendments rather than silently replacing the original note. These software
controls do not verify a doctor's professional license or the legal validity of a clinical signature.
Deployment. The approved public demonstration is a static Flutter Web application hosted on GitHub
Pages, with each browser keeping its own local SQLite data. A separate configuration can connect the
client to the Node.js shared API, but that pilot is incomplete. A real shared clinic system would require
an authoritative server, protected connections, managed secrets, backups and tested access controls.
The public demo should not be described as a live cloud medical-record service.

5.3 Database Design / Schema
5.3.1 Storage modes, schema version and integrity
The supplied web/demo_seed.sqlite snapshot was inspected directly. It uses schema version 35 and
contains 69 application tables. SQLite reported a successful quick_check and no foreign-key
violations. The snapshot includes 106 users (60 patients, 44 staff and two administrators), eight
departments, 892 appointments, 1,199 medical records, 2,181 laboratory values, 624 vital records and
624 invoices. These counts describe the supplied dataset, not a guaranteed result of running the seeder
again. Selected integrity triggers are installed by AppDatabase.installIntegrityRules.
The schema stores identifiers and many status values as TEXT, timestamps and counters as
INTEGER, selected measurements and local monetary fields as REAL, and file bytes as BLOB.
PatientProfiles.userId and StaffProfiles.userId link directly to Users.id. Some medical records have no
appointment_id because they represent standalone information. Foreign keys protect relationships



                                                                                                     31
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 39 / 61>
between rows, but other rules must still check whether a staff account is an eligible clinician or
whether two appointment times overlap. The shared API uses a different schema and should not be
confused with the local 69-table database.

5.3.3 Transactions, migrations, query efficiency and storage correctness
Transactions keep related changes together. Booking and consultation finalization must either save
all required rows or fail without a partial result. Selected signed notes, issued-document versions and
audit records are also protected by append-only or version rules. An outbox records notification work
to be attempted later, while an idempotency record allows the application to recognize a previously
completed request.
Database performance should be checked as the number of records increases. Patient history, clinician
schedules, laboratory values and staff tasks are common queries that may benefit from indexes
matching their filters and sort order. These improvements should be based on measured query plans
rather than assumed performance problems in the small synthetic demonstration.
Local billing stores some dinar amounts as SQLite REAL values. BillingRepositoryImpl converts
selected values to integer fils through _fils(double bhd) for comparison and provider requests.
Persisting integer fils throughout the local database would make exact financial calculations easier, but
it would require a migration and reconciliation tests. The shared payment endpoints already use
integer fils.
Storage differs by platform. The native implementation has encrypted local SQLite storage, while
the browser demo uses local browser data without equivalent encryption. Neither mode by itself
provides a synchronized, authoritative hospital record. A future shared solution would need explicit
rules for patient identity, consent, clinical amendments, offline changes and conflicts between devices.

5.3.4 ERD Interpretation and Data Integrity Controls
The ERD in Figure 5.4 focuses on the relationships most important to the main workflows: users and
their profiles, patients and appointments, patients and records, and staff tasks and histories. It is a
readable summary of the physical model; the complete table definitions remain in the source code.

5.4 User Interface Design
The interface design is described in DESIGN.md and docs/figma-redesign/implementation-map.json.
It uses blue actions, light backgrounds, white cards and dark text. Different status colors are supported
by words or icons so that urgency is not shown through color alone. Shared UI components follow a
4dp spacing scale and target minimum touch areas of 48dp. The design uses Lexend, Inter and Noto
Naskh Arabic. Navigation changes with screen width: bottom navigation on phones, a rail on tablets
and a wider sidebar on large screens.

AppScaffold provides a consistent layout for major screens, while AuthScaffold is used for sign-in and
registration. Reusable cards, navigation rows and action tiles keep similar information presented in a
consistent way. Lists display loading, empty and error states, and protected routes use GoRouter
guards. When a patient switches to a linked family member, the selected subject should remain clear
on every relevant screen.
The main interface journeys are straightforward. A patient signs in, checks records or upcoming
appointments, chooses a doctor and confirms a booking. For an uploaded document, the patient sees
the pending-review state before a clinician accepts or rejects it. A doctor moves from the daily
schedule to the patient chart, writes a draft and finalizes the consultation. An administrator reviews
operational requests and permitted approvals through the dashboard. These journeys are illustrated by
the screenshots in Chapter 6.
The design file contains 78 reference frames, but those frames should not be counted as 78
independently tested screens. Additional manual testing is still needed for Arabic medical terms, larger
text, assistive technology, task completion time and user satisfaction. The report therefore describes
these as usability goals rather than completed evaluation results.
Figure 5.5: Booking state progression through authorized repository operations



                                                                                                                          35

5.5 Chapter Summary
The overall architecture provides a clear boundary between the Flutter screens and application logic
and data access. It supports the most common local workflows, using a relational database and
transactional processing, while isolating shared-server integration as a separate and unfinished path.
Further work should focus on implementation of the remaining remote adapters, evaluation of
database performance and defining an explicit deployment contract before adding more complexity.

6.1 System Implementation Details
6.1.1 Tools, frameworks and selection rationale
Table 6.1: Actual implementation technology inventory
