The inspected project does not use Firebase Authentication, Firestore or Firebase Hosting as its main
platform. Its local data layer is Drift/SQLite, with a separate Node.js API pilot. Local passwords use
PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 120,000 iterations for ordinary accounts; the synthetic data generator
uses less expensive test hashes. Security properties differ between native and browser storage, so the
application should not be described as an encrypted live clinical service.

6.1.2 Implementation trace — identity, access and navigation
The application starts in main.dart and creates the Flutter interface through lib/app/app.dart. GoRouter
defines protected patient, staff and administrator routes in lib/app/router.dart. SessionController, in


                                                                                                                             38
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 46 / 61>
lib/features/auth/application/session.dart, tracks sign-in and permission changes and clears user-
specific state when necessary. AuthRepositoryImpl handles local credential checks and account
lockout. AccessPolicy then verifies the user's permitted patient or staff scope when records are read or
changed. These checks are applied below the screen level so that opening a route is not the only
security condition.
In shared mode, RemoteAuthRepository uses SharedClient.login to request a bearer session from
POST /api/login. The Node.js server checks the session and permissions for API actions. The client
also ignores stale responses after an account switch. Polling is used for some shared updates, but this
is not full real-time synchronization. Unsupported remote operations return an unavailable result rather
than quietly reading a different local dataset.

6.1.3 Implementation trace — transactional appointment allocation
AppointmentRepositoryImpl.book(BookingRequest) is responsible for saving a reservation. It first
checks whether the current account can manage the selected patient. It then uses a database transaction
to verify the slot's start and end, published schedule, exceptions and existing bookings. The same
transaction checks for a previous result with the request's idempotency key. If the slot remains valid, it
creates the appointment, assigns ticket details and records reminders or outbox work. The following
pseudocode summarizes these steps.

    book(request):
        actingAccount := authorizeBooking(request.patientId)
        if linkedPersonName is set but request targets actor's own record:
            return validation error
        TRANSACTION:
            if (same actor, scope and idempotency key) previously committed:
                return previously committed appointment
            require end > start and start > current time
            require interval belongs to clinician's published schedule
            require no availability exception overlaps interval
            require no existing appointment overlaps clinician interval
            require capacity >= 1
            assign deterministic ticket sequence and department room label
            INSERT appointment(patientId, staffId, interval, status, version,...)
            save idempotency-key-to-appointment reference
            create notification outbox and reminder schedule records
            return inserted appointment

The implementation uses _db.transaction, schedule-grid and exception checks, overlap checking and
IdempotencyGuard.prior/remember. These operations protect bookings stored in the same SQLite
database, including repeated requests. They cannot prevent a conflict between two separate browser
databases. A real shared appointment service must therefore make the server responsible for the final
booking decision.

6.1.4 Implementation trace — records, provenance and signed consultations
RecordRepositoryImpl.add(NewRecord) stores an imported medical record, related laboratory values
and source-file information. It validates supported file details and calculates a SHA-256 fingerprint to


                                                                                                       39
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 47 / 61>
identify duplicate content. Imported patient files are marked pendingReview until an authorized
clinician makes a review decision. RecordReads and RecordCorrections help preserve later history.
Because appointment_id may be empty, the timeline must also handle records that were not created
during a booked visit. File hashing confirms byte identity, not clinical accuracy.
EncounterDraftRepositoryImpl stores consultation drafts that can still be edited. When a clinician
finalizes a visit, EncounterRepositoryImpl.finalize validates the staff member and encounter state and
commits the signed note, linked records, medication orders and appointment changes together. The
draft is cleared after successful finalization. Later corrections use SignedNoteAmendments instead of
overwriting signed content. Clinical signatures and prescribing rights would still require formal
approval in a real clinic.

6.1.5 Implementation trace — rules-first staff risk workflow
RiskDetectionService reads selected records, vital signs, medicines and appointments through
repository interfaces. It applies defined rules for abnormal measurements, missing medication
coverage and overdue follow-up. A deduplication key helps prevent several tasks being created for the
same episode. TaskRepositoryImpl controls task ownership, status changes and history, while the staff
screen separates urgent, overdue, current and completed tasks. These functions support follow-up
work but do not amount to a validated diagnosis or triage system.

6.1.6 Implementation trace — AI summaries and no-show model
The application defines an AiService interface with MockAiService for offline examples and
GeminiAiService as an optional provider integration. PatientContextBuilder prepares information for a
summary, and AiSummaryController tracks whether the source context has changed. The capability
registry keeps live-clinical-ai and no-show-risk disabled in the approved demonstration. This matters
because external AI requests involving real medical data would need a secure server boundary, clinical
review and appropriate handling of patient information.
No-show      prediction.     The    Dart     service    lib/services/ml/no_show_predictor.dart   loads
assets/models/no_show_model.json through NoShowModel.load(). The JSON contains 11 feature
names, scaling values, model coefficients, an intercept and thresholds for risk bands. Each feature is
standardized using the training values and then contributes to a logistic-regression score, summarized
by the following equation:
                         z = b + SUM(i = 1..11) [w_i * (x_i - mean_i) / scale_i]
                                     P(no-show) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
NoShowModel.predict calculates the standardized feature contributions, applies the sigmoid function
and places the probability into a low, medium or high risk band. The 11 inputs include previous no-
show rate, booking lead time, first-visit status, chronic-condition flag, previous appointment count,
acknowledged reminders, hour and day, two visit-type indicators and age. The feature contributions




                                                                                                   40
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 48 / 61>
describe how the model calculates a score; they do not prove why an individual patient might miss a
visit.
The synthetic evaluation in docs/ml_results.md used 2,145 held-out appointments, of which 25.1%
were no-shows. Reported results were accuracy 0.733, precision 0.476, recall 0.623, F1 score 0.540
and ROC-AUC 0.754. The confusion matrix contained 1,236 true negatives, 370 false positives, 203
false negatives and 336 true positives. A majority-class baseline achieved 0.749 accuracy but did not
identify missed visits. This shows why accuracy alone is insufficient for an imbalanced dataset. The
reported model has not been independently reevaluated here or tested with real patients.

6.1.7 Documents, billing and notification state machines
DocumentServiceImpl handles document requests through preparation, submission, approval,
issuance, rendering and delivery. At issuance, the application saves the patient, issuer, language and
template content in IssuedDocumentVersions. The generated PDF is tracked separately in
DocumentArtifacts,     including     success   or   failure   information.   DocumentVerifications      and
DocumentDeliveryEvents record selected checks and attempts. These measures help preserve
document history, but official medical-document approval would require external policy and clinical
review.
BillingRepositoryImpl manages invoices, payment transactions, wallet entries, saved payment
descriptions and simulated gateway charges. Request references support safe retries, while separate
states record authorization, settlement or failure. Only masked card details are stored by the local
demonstration. The payment gateway is simulated, not connected to a live bank. Some local amounts
use REAL dinar values, with _fils(double bhd) converting selected calculations to integer fils. A future
migration to integer-fils storage would improve consistency.
Notification records are written through an outbox so that a successful database change can be
followed by a delivery attempt. An outbox entry confirms that the application intends to send a
message; it does not prove that an SMS or push notification reached the user. The demonstration
should keep this difference clear.

6.2 Testing & Results
6.2.1 Testing strategy and evidence classification
Testing covers different levels of the application. Unit tests check calculations and rules, widget tests
check forms and navigation, and database tests examine transactions, relationships and migrations.
Integration and security tests cover selected user journeys, server requests, access denial and repeated
actions. The repository stores Dart tests under test/, Flutter integration tests under integration_test/ and
separate Node.js API tests. Static analysis and code-generation tools provide additional checks.
Table 6.2 distinguishes five kinds of evidence. A direct pass was checked in the technical review. A
repository-reported pass was recorded by the team but not rerun during this review. A partial run

produced some observed results without finishing the full suite. Source-supported means the test or
feature exists but was not independently executed. Open indicates an unfinished acceptance or
deployment task. This prevents an existing test file from being counted automatically as a passing test.

6.2.3 Analysis of testing completeness and research results
The SQLite checks show that the supplied database is structurally valid, but they do not prove that
every medical value or permission is correct. The repository contains many automated tests; to
confirm the current release, the full suite still needs to run on a documented toolchain and commit.
Manual acceptance should include failed actions as well as successful ones, such as a revoked family
link, a rejected import, a declined simulated payment, a draft conflict and an Arabic document that
cannot be displayed correctly.
RQ1 is demonstrated by collecting a patient's records into a timeline and producing offline example
summaries. The accuracy of those summaries has not been measured against clinician-reviewed
answers. A future evaluation should check completeness, incorrect statements, contradictions and
whether each statement can be traced to a source record.
RQ2 includes a synthetic no-show prediction experiment. The reported ROC-AUC of 0.754 suggests
useful ranking within that synthetic dataset, while precision of 0.476 and F1 of 0.540 show that errors
remain. The model is disabled for routine use, and the project has not measured a reduction in real
missed appointments. Before operational use, the model would need evaluation on representative data,
calibration, fairness checks and testing of the intervention it would support.


                                                                                                                              44
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 52 / 61>
RQ3 is demonstrated by rule-based risk flags and staff task management. Suitable tests include
checking whether each rule fires on the intended input, whether repeated events create duplicate tasks,
and whether assignments and escalations respect permissions. These checks are different from proving
that clinical diagnoses or patient outcomes have improved. A later user study could also measure how
quickly staff find and finish important tasks.

6.2.4 Verification commands and reproducibility
To rerun the checks, use the versions specified in toolchain.json and the Node.js requirement recorded
in the repository. Run the following commands from a clean copy, then record the commit, operating
system, tool versions and exit status for each command:

    flutter --version
    flutter pub get
    dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
    dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed lib test integration_test
    flutter analyze
    flutter test
    flutter build web --dart-define=APP_MODE=demo
    # In the shared service directory, use the repository's own test instructions
    # and pinned Node 24.13.0; do not mistake a partial timeout for a clean pass.

Database verification should record SQLite user_version, quick_check, foreign_key_check and
representative query plans. Browser checks should cover patient, doctor and administrator journeys,
including expected access denials. Use synthetic accounts only; real patient records must not be placed
in the public demo.

6.2.5 Visual Functional Evidence from the Synthetic Demo
Figures 6.1–6.5 are screenshots included in the MyHealth Care repository. They show the main
interface layouts used by patients and staff. A screenshot is useful evidence of visual design, but a
successful database operation still needs a separate functional test. The images in this report use
synthetic information.

The final demonstration should cover three complete journeys: uploading and reviewing a patient
record, booking an appointment and finalizing a consultation, and detecting a risk flag and completing
the related staff task. Each should use synthetic data and show both the action and the saved result.
The team should also explain that the AI experiment and shared-server pilot are not approved clinical
services.

6.4 Chapter Summary
The implementation provides a broad local demonstration and a smaller shared-server pilot. Its
database design, service boundaries and test coverage are substantial for a senior project. However,
full independent build verification, user testing, clinical approval and complete shared-mode operation
remain outstanding. The screenshots support the explanation of the interface but do not replace
executable test evidence.




                                                                                                              49
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 57 / 61>
                                     Chapter 7
                            Conclusion and Future Work
7.1 Introduction
This chapter summarizes the system that has been built and displays evidence towards its main
objectives. It also highlights the limitations of the current prototype, and what requirements its needs
in order to be extended to outside the university demonstration.

7.2 Summary of the Project
MyHealth Care has been built as a Flutter/Dart application with separate workspaces for patient, staff
and admin. Patients have the option of looking at their records and appointments, clinical staff can
manage consultations, imported results, issued items and actions, all stored in a structured relational
database with transactional booking, permissions checks, review states and a history of signed notes.
Riverpod, GoRouter and the repository interface bring a separation between the user interface and
application rules and store, which are presumably going to make this prototype more testable and
sustainable.

7.3 Key Findings and Results
The local database under test uses schema version 35 and spans 69 interconnected tables. It was able
to pass read-only SQLite integrity and foreign-key validation checks. Although the repository contains
a comprehensive collection of automated tests, the entire suite of Flutter tests was not run on its own
during this report's investigation. The Node.js shared API provides a suggestion of how a server-
backed version may look, but it is not yet integrated into the app.

7.4 Significance of the Project
Three separate research pathways are integrated in the prototype: patient history and demonstration
summary organization; a no-show prediction experiment; and rule-based staff task management. The
0.754 ROC-AUC score cited for the predictor is achieved using synthetic data and does not
demonstrate performance in a real clinical environment. The conclusion is therefore more about
technical implementation and workflow design, rather than real decrease in waiting times, cancellation
rate, and medical errors.

7.5 Limitations of the System
My Health Care is not a certified electronic health record and not a deployed clinical service. No
customer verified hospital interoperability. No real patient verified identity. External notifications, full
shared-server coverage, clinical AI approved, multi-device support are still a work in progress. Some
platform and backend tests require a full, recorded rerun. This needs to be explicitly mentioned in the
demos.




                                                                                                         50
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 58 / 61>
7.6 Implications of the Project
The project shows that the area of patient history, appointment booking and follow-up of staff can be
arranged in one role-based Flutter application quite successfully. A lot of the senior project are due to
the workflow, database rules and evidence of technical tests. Claims on any real benefit for the
patients would require user studies and clinical trials well outside the scope of the prototype.

7.7 Future Work
7.7.1 Graduation Demonstration and Documentation
Graduation priorities. For graduation, the following are the priorities: stability of the synthetic
browser demo, update the README/diagrams to match implementation, document the results of a full
test run. We want to see the main workflows in either Arabic or English (with keyboards and large
text). The team should be able to show the tasks for a patient, doctor, and admin without needing any
real patient data or leaving any hard-to-decode external dependencies.

7.7.2 Controlled Multi-Device Pilot
Shared-server pilot. requires the remaining remote repository adapters and the same set of checked-
in enabled actions by the server. For private deployment, use HTTPS, persistent storage, back ups,
monitoring, secret management, tested recoveries. For a private deployment with shared schema
version 2, handle all critical use cases such as two bookings for the same slot, changes to permissions
while the request is open, repeated payment or document requests. Declare only explicit integration
plan for local schema version 35 and shared schema version 2 rather than rely on implicit schema
version 2 sync.

7.7.3 Health Data Interoperability
Interoperability. Patient and prescription records can then be linked to the specified HL7 FHIR
(Health Level Seven International, n.d.) resources and standards using a future project with a
healthcare provider. This task will necessitate agreeing on patient matching, consent standards,
terminology, provenance and data quality. However, a standards-based approach does not necessarily
ensure the equivalence or correctness of clinical records from different providers.

7.7.4 Clinical Decision Support Research
AI evaluation. Next steps should be to evaluate summaries on clinician-reviewed records for
omissions or unsubstantiated claims. Evaluation of no-show predictions would be required on
representative data to assess calibration and fairness, before testing the reminder interventions. Risk-
rule alerts should be analyzed for false warnings, and effects on staff workload. Automated diagnosis
may be potential, but requires caution, professional review, ethical approval, and independent
validation (World Health Organization, 2021a).




                                                                                                      51
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 59 / 61>
7.7.5 Patient Engagement and Wearables
Patient services. potential improvements could involve the addition of telehealth, verified reminders,
medication follow-up, digital consent and optional wearable measurements. Wearable measurements
must be verified, correctly timed, and recorded to the clinical history before uploading into a central
database. Transition to larger cloud storage or PostgreSQL should be driven by storage capacity needs
and operational use-case; security and backup issues should be considered.

7.7.6 Long-Term Governance and Research
Long-term maintenance. Future research will define the classification of code changes, migration,
API compatibility, security testing, and release note updates. If this project is evaluated with real
participants, the research will need to follow an approved procedure and report participant recruitment,
task times, errors, and methods used. The system will be referred to as the synthetic-data prototype in
the case of no such evaluation.

7.8 Conclusion
MyHealth Care project supports its main objective of a senior project by presenting the role-based
patient and clinic flows in an operational synthetic-data application. Among the most impressive
features of this application are handling of related clinical records, conflict-aware appointment
scheduling, repository-level permission checking, and staff task tracking. The system as it stands is
suitable for academic demonstration but limited and should be thoroughly described. Further technical
development, user testing, and approval are needed for use in a real clinical environment.
